crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Curriculum and Learning Outcomes covers the design of a course as a sequence of intended capabilities, and the statements used to check whether those capabilities were reached. It sits inside course design and teaching, where it connects subject matter expertise to assessment, sequencing and time on task. The scope runs from a single module's objectives to a full programme's graduate attributes, and it includes the mapping that shows how one supports the other. It also covers the vocabulary of outcomes, competences, standards and rubrics, which are often used loosely and interchangeably in practice.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a syllabus or course outline, a set of outcome statements, and an assessment plan that ties each statement to evidence. Institutions usually hold these in a learning management system, a curriculum mapping tool or a programme handbook, with version control handled by a committee rather than a single author. Accreditation bodies and internal quality offices supply the frameworks and reporting templates that shape what gets written down. Reading lists, textbooks and the site's own catalogue of 91 AI books are typical supporting material for a course in this field.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Design usually starts from the end, with what a graduate should be able to do, then works backwards to assessments and only then to teaching activities. Outcomes are written as observable verbs so that two markers can agree on whether they were met, and rubrics spell out the levels between not yet and proficient. Mapping exercises trace each outcome to the modules and assessments that deliver it, which exposes gaps and accidental repetition. Review cycles, often annual, compare student evidence against the stated aims and revise the statements or the teaching accordingly.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Ownership sits with the programme team and the institution's quality office, and changes to published outcomes normally require formal approval. Records of what was taught, what was assessed and what students achieved are kept for accreditation and for appeals, so provenance matters as much as the wording. Assessment design has to account for fairness across cohorts, accessibility, and the risk that a narrow outcome set narrows what gets taught. Where a course draws on published research, the site links to the original paper rather than to a search tool, which keeps the citation trail intact.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Programmes are moving toward smaller, stackable credentials and toward outcomes expressed as demonstrable skills rather than hours of contact. Employers and professional bodies increasingly ask for evidence of competence, which pushes assessment toward portfolios and authentic tasks. Generative tools are forcing teams to restate outcomes so that they describe judgement and process, not just a finished artefact. The open question is how much standardisation is useful before it starts to crowd out the local knowledge that makes a course worth teaching.
